Today's śloka card is simpler: just the verse and where it is from. Save, Another śloka and Word by word are under the ⋯ button.
The bottom bar no longer has Read (it is still in the top menu and on the Home page).
Settings are grouped and show a preview verse, so you see what a change does.
New: Settings → Downloads. Save a kāṇḍa or parva at a time to read without internet, and remove it again.

New in the Pariśiṣṭa: Characters. 42 people of the Rāmāyaṇa and 81 of the Mahābhārata, each with their role, a short description in Kannada and English, a circle of their relations, key moments that open the verse, and family trees of the main lines.
In word-by-word meanings, a name links to that character's page.
Tighter reading layout: each verse starts with its reference and metre in one row, and the text uses the full width of the screen.
The four work buttons are in two rows with their full names, and the verse of the day no longer runs off the edge on the Mahābhārata page.

New fonts, the same as the Kāvya app: Noto Serif Kannada (or Noto Sans Kannada, in Options), Noto Serif Devanagari and Cormorant Garamond. Verses are set a little bolder and tighter, with the second half-line indented and the dandas in colour.
The “Classical pañcama” switch (ಪುಙ್ಗವ for ಪುಂಗವ) now changes the Kannada text only.
The app's address is now ramayana-blond.vercel.app; shared verse cards show it. The old github.io copy is no longer updated.
In the chant view's Page layout each śloka now starts on its own line, so the end of one verse no longer runs into the beginning of the next (the PDF export does the same).

The Bhagavadgītā's Traditional text was proofread: 228 typing slips in the digital source are corrected (for example a stray “ka” after words, aśrute for aśnute). Each corrected verse shows what changed under its details.
Kannada script now shows the anusvāra before a consonant of its own class (ಸಂಗ, ಪಂಚ), as Kannada books print it. The Homorganic nasals option still shows ಸಙ್ಗ, ಪಞ್ಚ.
Semicolons and hyphens from the digital sources no longer appear inside Mahābhārata verses, and many more Pune verses now have their metre named.
Gītā 13.26 and 13.27 are shown as two verses again, and in 1.21 and 1.28 “arjuna uvāca” stands where it belongs, inside the verse.

New: the Bhagavadgītā, as a third button beside the two epics. Read its 18 adhyāyas in the Traditional (Kumbakonam) or Pune text, with the speaker shown above each verse, chapter names, chant view, search and a verse of the day.
The Gītā Dhyāna ślokas, the nine verses recited before the Gītā, open the Gītā section.
Mahābhārata pages that contain the Gītā link to it, and each Gītā verse links back to its place in the Mahābhārata.
Fixed: two Pune Mahābhārata verses (Bhīṣma Parva 23.1 and 40.78) carried extra text from the digital source that is not part of the epic.

New Pariśiṣṭa (appendix) button beside the two epics. Its first section, Chandas, lists the metres found in the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata: how each is built, how many verses use it in each kāṇḍa or parva, and verses to read, linked to the text.
“Parvan” is now spelled “Parva”.
The work buttons, kāṇḍa and parva cards, headings and menus now follow the script you choose at the top (Kannada, Devanāgarī or Roman) instead of always showing Kannada.
Going to the Dictionary from a word card and coming back (Back button, or the ← button in the Dictionary) returns you to the same verse with the same word's card open.
The Dictionary now follows Itihāsa's light or dark setting.
A Dictionary button in the bottom bar opens the Śabdārtha Kaustubha Sanskrit–Kannada dictionary (46,800 words) inside Itihāsa, with search and browsing; it works offline once opened.
In the word-by-word panel, tap a word to see its dictionary entry under it: Kannada meanings, derivation and a link to the full entry.
A new Kosha button in the bottom bar opens the Śabdārtha Kaustubha Sanskrit–Kannada dictionary (from the VedaAlokana project) in a new tab.

The Mahābhārata now has word-by-word meanings. Open the icon beside a verse of the Pune text to see each word with its grammar and meaning; verses of the Traditional text that match a Pune verse show the same analysis.
The two Mahābhārata texts are now linked verse by verse: see the same verse in the other text, hide verses that are not in it, and notes where the readings differ.

Kannada meanings appear for about 500 names, epithets and small words in both epics when the script is Kannada. They were written by Claude and are waiting for a Kannada reader to review them. The Bhagavadgītā has no word-by-word analysis yet; the pages say so.

Each kāṇḍa and parvan card now has three paintings: the temple niche, a Kalamkari-style motif and a Pattachitra-style motif, each from that book's story. Every time you open the app a new mix is shown; it stays the same while you read.
The work chips mix their icons the same way: bow and arrow, pādukā or setu for the Rāmāyaṇa; Sudarśana chakra, Pāñcajanya or flute and peacock feather for the Mahābhārata.

The app is now called ಇತಿಹಾಸ (Itihāsa). Choosing between the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata is two chips at the top of Home and Read: a bow and arrow for the Rāmāyaṇa, the Sudarśana chakra for the Mahābhārata.
New app icon background, blending the two works' colours.

The Mahābhārata is now in the app as a second work: choose it from the chip under the greeting on Home and Read. It has the same reading, chant, search, saved verses, offline packs and daily śloka as the Rāmāyaṇa.
Two texts: Traditional Text (Kumbakonam, 96,415 verses) and Pune Text (critical edition, 73,821 verses), in 18 parvans with painted cards.
Your place, saved verses, today's śloka and the texts switched on are kept separately for each work; script letter, text size and theme apply to both.
Word-by-word meanings and links between the two texts are not available for the Mahābhārata yet.
Swipe sideways to move to the next or previous sarga: one finger in the reading view, two fingers in the chant view (one finger there still moves by verse).
Today's śloka is now a palm-leaf manuscript card, with round icons for another, save, word by word, share and open.
Home: Continue reading and Begin are now one card, with a small play icon to begin and an arrow to resume.
New look: a greeting Home, a Read tab and a floating tab bar.
Kāṇḍas are shown as temple-painting cards; tap one to pick a sarga.
Pick your script with one letter: ಅ, अ or A. Reading settings open from the sliders button.
A new app icon.
Every verse has a small word-by-word icon beside its number. Tap it to open the meanings; it is dimmed when a verse has none.
Click or tap any verse in the reading view to see its words with grammar and meanings. Traditional verses that differ a little from the Baroda verse show its analysis with a note.
The Traditional Text is now the default; the Baroda Text is optional and can be turned on in Options.
Word by word now also works on Traditional Text verses that match a Baroda verse.
Home no longer has the Editions section or the My list button; the phone tab bar has Home, Search and My.
Light is now the default look. Options has a Theme choice: Light, Dark, or Same as device.
The two texts have clearer names: Baroda Text (the Critical Edition) and Traditional Text (the Vulgate).
Options now lets you switch either text off, so lists, search and links show only the one you read. At least one stays on.
New Chant view: a full-screen reading mode with a book page and one verse at a time, text size, script and layout controls, swipes and keys. Closing it returns you to where you started.
Print and PDF of the chant view, in the script you chose. On phones the PDF is shared as a file.
New Home: verse of the day (365 verses, a different one each day, with words, metre and context), Continue reading, kāṇḍa tiles with sarga chips, My list.
Works offline once installed. Pages you have read are kept; whole kāṇḍas can be downloaded from About.
Bottom tab bar on phones, a side list of kāṇḍas on wide screens, and a Back button that never leaves the site.
Word-by-word analysis of Critical Edition verses, with dictionary senses of each word.
The traditional Vulgate as a second edition, with verse-by-verse links to the Critical Edition.
Critical Edition reader in Kannada script, Devanāgarī and IAST, with search and citations.
